cases.title: Acute Chest Pain in Middle-Aged Man
learning_objectives: Differentiate acute coronary syndrome from other causes of chest pain
Apply HEART score for risk stratification
cases.presentation: 55-year-old man with sudden-onset crushing chest pain radiating to left arm, associated with diaphoresis and dyspnea

history.hpi: Patient was mowing lawn when developed severe substernal chest pressure. Pain radiates to left arm and jaw. Associated with shortness of breath and sweating. No relief with rest.
history.social: Smoking 1 PPD x 30 years, occasional alcohol

labs.ecg: ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF

cases.explanation: This is a classic presentation of inferior STEMI. Key features include: (1) Cardiac risk factors (smoking, HTN, DM, HLD, family history), (2) Classic anginal chest pain with radiation, (3) Associated symptoms (diaphoresis, dyspnea), (4) Elevated troponin, (5) ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Time is muscle - activate cath lab immediately!
management_pearls: MONA: Morphine, Oxygen (if hypoxic), Nitroglycerin, Aspirin 325mg
Activate cath lab for emergent PCI (door-to-balloon <90 min)
Dual antiplatelet therapy: Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel)
Anticoagulation: Heparin or bivalirudin
Beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor within 24 hours
High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg)
cases.author: Dr. Teaching Attending

cases.title: Young Woman with Severe Headache
learning_objectives: Recognize red flags for secondary headache
cases.presentation: 28-year-old woman with sudden-onset 'worst headache of life', associated with neck stiffness and photophobia

history.hpi: Patient was at work when suddenly developed explosive headache. Describes it as 'thunderclap' - reached maximum intensity within seconds. Associated with nausea, vomiting, and neck pain. No trauma.
history.pmh: Migraine headaches (different character), no previous similar episodes

physical_exam.neuro: Alert and oriented, cranial nerves intact, no focal deficits

imaging.lp: Opening pressure 25 cm H2O, RBC 50,000 (tube 1) and 48,000 (tube 4), xanthochromia present

cases.explanation: Classic subarachnoid hemorrhage presentation: 'thunderclap headache' (sudden, severe, maximal at onset), meningismus (neck stiffness), photophobia. CT shows blood in basilar cisterns. LP confirms SAH with persistent RBCs and xanthochromia (breakdown of hemoglobin). Key is recognizing 'worst headache of life' red flag.
management_pearls: Immediate neurosurgery consult
CT angiography to identify aneurysm source
Nimodipine 60mg q4h to prevent vasospasm
Blood pressure control: SBP <160 mmHg (avoid hypotension)
Serial neuro exams for deterioration
Prevent rebleeding: early aneurysm securement (coiling or clipping)
cases.author: Dr. Neurology Attending

cases.title: Elderly Man with Fever and Productive Cough
learning_objectives: Apply CURB-65 score for severity assessment
cases.presentation: 72-year-old man with 3 days of fever, productive cough with green sputum, and shortness of breath

history.hpi: Patient developed fever, chills, and productive cough 3 days ago. Sputum is green-yellow. Associated with pleuritic chest pain on right side. Progressive dyspnea.
history.social: Former smoker (quit 5 years ago), 40 pack-year history

physical_exam.lungs: Decreased breath sounds right lower lobe, crackles, egophony

cases.explanation: Community-acquired pneumonia with typical presentation: fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, tachypnea. Physical exam shows focal findings (crackles, egophony). CXR confirms consolidation. CURB-65 score: 2 points (age >65, elevated BUN) suggests moderate severity requiring hospitalization.
management_pearls: CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65
Empiric antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin or respiratory fluoroquinolone
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >90%
IV fluids for hydration
Blood cultures before antibiotics
Consider MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage if risk factors present
references: Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults: Diagnosis and Management
cases.author: Dr. Pulmonology Attending

cases.title: Young Adult with Abdominal Pain
learning_objectives: Differentiate surgical vs non-surgical acute abdomen
cases.presentation: 22-year-old man with 12 hours of progressive right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and fever

history.hpi: Pain started periumbilically this morning, then migrated to RLQ. Worsening over time. Associated with anorexia, nausea, one episode of vomiting. No diarrhea. Pain worse with movement.

physical_exam.abdomen: RLQ tenderness maximal at McBurney's point, rebound and guarding present, positive Rovsing's sign

imaging.ct_abdomen: Dilated appendix 12mm with periappendiceal fat stranding

cases.explanation: Classic acute appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to RLQ, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis. Physical exam findings (McBurney's point tenderness, rebound, guarding, Rovsing's sign) strongly suggest appendicitis. CT confirms diagnosis. Alvarado score ≥7 indicates high probability requiring surgical consultation.
management_pearls: NPO and IV fluids for resuscitation
Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin-tazobactam
Pain control: IV opioids after surgical evaluation
Urgent surgical consultation for appendectomy
Laparoscopic preferred over open if available
Single-dose pre-operative antibiotics if uncomplicated
references: JAMA: Appendicitis - Clinical Manifestations and Diagnosis
World Society of Emergency Surgery guidelines for appendicitis
cases.author: Dr. General Surgery Attending

cases.title: Diabetic Patient with Altered Mental Status
cases.presentation: 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presenting with confusion, polyuria, and abdominal pain

history.chief_complaint: My daughter is confused and breathing fast
history.hpi: Patient ran out of insulin 3 days ago. Developed polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Today became confused and lethargic. Fruity breath odor noted by family.
history.medications: Insulin glargine, insulin lispac (ran out 3 days ago)

cases.explanation: Classic DKA triad: hyperglycemia (>250), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarb <18), and ketonemia. Precipitating factor: insulin non-compliance. Clinical features include Kussmaul respirations (respiratory compensation), fruity breath (acetone), dehydration, altered mental status, and abdominal pain (pseudoperitonitis).
management_pearls: ABC stabilization: 2 large-bore IVs, oxygen if needed
Aggressive IV fluids: 1L NS bolus, then 250-500 mL/hr
Insulin infusion: 0.1 units/kg/hr (DO NOT give bolus if K+ <3.3)
Potassium replacement crucial: monitor q2-4h (K+ drops with insulin)
When glucose <250: switch to D5 1/2 NS, continue insulin until anion gap closes
Identify precipitating cause: infection, MI, non-compliance most common
Bicarbonate only if pH <6.9 (controversial)
Transition to subQ insulin when: eating, anion gap normal, pH >7.3
references: ADA: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults with Diabetes
cases.author: Dr. Emergency Medicine Attending

cases.title: Febrile Child with Stiff Neck
cases.presentation: 18-month-old girl with fever, irritability, and decreased oral intake brought by worried parents

history.chief_complaint: High fever and won't stop crying
history.hpi: Fever to 103°F for 12 hours. Progressive irritability. Vomiting twice. Decreased PO intake. Parents note child cries when picked up. No known sick contacts. Immunizations up to date.

physical_exam.neck: Nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs
physical_exam.skin: Petechial rash on trunk and extremities

labs.lp: Opening pressure 28 cm H2O, WBC 3,500 (90% PMNs), protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 25 mg/dL

imaging.ct_head: No mass effect, LP safe to perform

cases.explanation: Bacterial meningitis: fever, altered mental status, meningismus (nuchal rigidity, Kernig/Brudzinski signs). Petechial rash suggests Neisseria meningitidis. CSF shows: elevated WBC with PMN predominance, elevated protein, low glucose. Classic CSF formula: 'High cells, high protein, low glucose' = bacterial. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate antibiotics.
management_pearls: Do NOT delay antibiotics for LP if unstable or coagulopathy
Empiric antibiotics STAT: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (add ampicillin if <1 month or >50 years for Listeria)
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg before/with first antibiotic dose (reduces mortality)
Aggressive IV fluids and supportive care
Droplet precautions until bacterial meningitis ruled out
Prophylaxis for close contacts if N. meningitidis confirmed (rifampin or cipro)
Monitor for complications: increased ICP, seizures, SIADH, septic shock
references: IDSA Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis
Pediatric Bacterial Meningitis: Recognition and Management
cases.author: Dr. Pediatric Emergency Medicine

cases.title: Man with Sudden Severe Back Pain
cases.presentation: 68-year-old man with sudden-onset severe abdominal and back pain, feeling lightheaded

history.hpi: Sudden onset severe abdominal pain radiating to back 1 hour ago while lifting groceries. Describes tearing sensation. Feels dizzy. Wife notes he looks pale and sweaty.
history.pmh: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, known 5cm AAA on surveillance
history.social: Former smoker (quit 10 years ago), 50 pack-year history

physical_exam.abdomen: Tender, pulsatile mass, guarding, no bowel sounds

imaging.bedside_us: Large AAA with hypoechoic rim, free fluid in abdomen

cases.explanation: Ruptured AAA: classic triad of abdominal/back pain, hypotension, and pulsatile abdominal mass. Risk factors present: known AAA, age >65, male, smoking history, HTN. Grey-Turner sign (flank ecchymosis) indicates retroperitoneal hemorrhage. This is immediately life-threatening. Do NOT delay for CT if unstable - go directly to OR!
management_pearls: CALL VASCULAR SURGERY IMMEDIATELY - this is a surgical emergency
Permissive hypotension: Target SBP 80-100 (avoid overresuscitation causing more bleeding)
Massive transfusion protocol: 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets
2 large-bore IVs, type and cross 10 units PRBC
Do NOT delay for CT if hemodynamically unstable - STAT to OR
Endovascular repair (EVAR) preferred if anatomy suitable and available
Mortality 50% even with surgery - counsel family
Post-op complications: renal failure, bowel ischemia, compartment syndrome
references: SVS Practice Guidelines for Ruptured AAA
Emergency Management of Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
cases.author: Dr. Vascular Surgery

cases.title: Woman with Painful Swollen Leg
cases.presentation: 45-year-old woman with 2 days of left leg pain and swelling after long flight from Europe

history.chief_complaint: My left leg is swollen and hurts
history.hpi: Returned from 10-hour flight 3 days ago. Left calf started hurting 2 days ago. Progressive swelling. Pain worse with walking. No trauma. No chest pain or shortness of breath.

physical_exam.extremities: Left calf swollen, 3cm larger than right, tender to palpation, warm, positive Homan's sign

imaging.doppler_ultrasound: Non-compressible left popliteal and femoral veins, intraluminal echogenic material consistent with thrombus

cases.explanation: Provoked DVT with multiple risk factors: recent prolonged travel (>8 hours), OCPs, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history. Wells score: leg swelling (1), calf tenderness (1), entire leg swollen (1), recently bedridden/surgery (1.5) = 4.5 points = DVT likely. Ultrasound confirms non-compressible vein with thrombus.
management_pearls: Anticoagulation immediately: Apixaban 10mg BID x 7 days, then 5mg BID OR Rivaroxaban 15mg BID x 21 days, then 20mg daily
Alternative: Enoxaparin 1mg/kg BID bridge to warfarin (if DOACs contraindicated)
Discontinue estrogen-containing contraceptives (thrombogenic)
Compression stockings for symptom relief (not proven to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome)
Encourage early mobilization (bedrest not recommended)
Screen for PE: ask about chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis
Duration: Minimum 3 months, consider extended if unprovoked
Repeat ultrasound at 1 week if symptoms worsen (rule out extension)
references: Diagnosis and Management of Acute Deep Vein Thrombosis
cases.author: Dr. Vascular Medicine

cases.title: Elderly Woman Feeling Weak and Tired
cases.presentation: 62-year-old woman with several months of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and constipation

history.hpi: Progressive fatigue over 6 months. Gained 15 lbs without dietary changes. Feels cold even in warm rooms. Constipation worsening. Dry skin. Hair thinning. Depressed mood.

physical_exam.neuro: Delayed deep tendon reflexes (slow relaxation phase)

imaging.thyroid_us: Heterogeneous echotexture consistent with chronic thyroiditis

cases.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism (likely Hashimoto's thyroiditis based on positive anti-TPO antibodies). Classic symptoms: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, delayed reflexes. Labs show elevated TSH with low free T4. Hypercholesterolemia is common secondary finding.
management_pearls: Levothyroxine: Start 1.6 mcg/kg/day (round to 50, 75, 88, 100 mcg tablets)
Take on empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before breakfast
Recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks, adjust dose by 12.5-25 mcg increments
Goal TSH: 0.5-2.5 mIU/L (lower end for young patients)
Elderly/cardiac disease: Start low (25 mcg), go slow (risk of precipitating MI)
Drug interactions: Iron, calcium, PPIs decrease absorption (separate by 4 hours)
Monitor symptoms and TSH every 6-12 months once stable
Lifelong therapy required in most cases
cases.author: Dr. Endocrinology

cases.title: Man with Sudden Vision Loss
cases.presentation: 65-year-old man with sudden, painless loss of vision in right eye 1 hour ago

history.chief_complaint: I can't see out of my right eye
history.hpi: Sudden onset complete vision loss in right eye while reading newspaper. Painless. No preceding symptoms. No trauma. No flashing lights or floaters. Left eye vision normal.

physical_exam.eye_exam: Right eye: Light perception only, RAPD present, fundoscopy shows pale retina with cherry red spot at macula

cases.explanation: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO): sudden, painless, complete vision loss. Classic fundoscopic finding is cherry red spot (fovea has dual blood supply, stands out against pale ischemic retina). This is an ocular stroke - 'time is retina'. RAPD confirms afferent pupillary defect. Risk factors: AFib (embolic), carotid stenosis, smoking, HTN. ESR not markedly elevated, making GCA less likely.
management_pearls: THIS IS AN EMERGENCY - Permanent vision loss occurs after 90-100 minutes
Immediate ophthalmology consult
Ocular massage: Firm pressure on eye for 5 sec, release 5 sec, repeat x 5 cycles
Anterior chamber paracentesis (by ophthalmology) to lower IOP
Hyperbaric oxygen if available and <24 hours from onset
ASA 325mg (prevent recurrence)
Start anticoagulation for AFib (warfarin or DOAC)
Workup embolic source: Echo, carotid ultrasound
Consider CEA if severe carotid stenosis (>70%)
Visual recovery poor even with treatment (15-30%)
references: AAO Acute Retinal Artery Occlusion Guidelines
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion: Diagnosis and Management
cases.author: Dr. Ophthalmology

cases.title: Hypotensive Patient with Fever and Altered Mental Status
cases.presentation: 58-year-old man brought by ambulance with fever, confusion, and low blood pressure

history.chief_complaint: Found confused at home with fever
history.hpi: Family found patient confused this morning. Had urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency) for 3 days but didn't seek care. Now febrile, lethargic, and incontinent of urine.

physical_exam.general: Lethargic, responds to painful stimuli only
physical_exam.skin: Mottled, cool extremities, delayed cap refill >4 seconds

cases.explanation: Septic shock from urosepsis: SIRS criteria met (temp >38°C, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12k with bandemia). Hypotension refractory to fluids + elevated lactate = septic shock. Source is urinary (UA findings, suprapubic tenderness). Organ dysfunction: AKI (Cr elevated), altered mental status, hypoxia. qSOFA score 3 (AMS, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100) predicts high mortality.
management_pearls: HOUR-1 BUNDLE (start immediately):
1. Measure lactate (remeasure if >2)
2. Obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics
3. Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour: Pip-tazo or cefepime + vancomycin
4. 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension/lactate ≥4
5. Vasopressors if hypotensive during/after fluid resuscitation (target MAP ≥65)
Norepinephrine is first-line vasopressor
Source control: Foley catheter (relieve obstruction), consider urology consult
Monitor: Central line, arterial line, continuous vitals
ICU admission for close monitoring
Steroid (hydrocortisone 200mg/day) if vasopressor-dependent
references: Recognition and Management of Septic Shock
cases.author: Dr. Critical Care

cases.title: Man with Sudden Right-Sided Weakness
cases.presentation: 67-year-old man with sudden onset right-sided weakness and slurred speech 90 minutes ago

history.chief_complaint: Right side not working, can't talk right
history.hpi: Wife reports patient was fine at breakfast. Suddenly developed right arm/leg weakness and difficulty speaking at 8:00 AM. Last known normal time 7:30 AM (90 min ago). No seizure, no head trauma. EMS activated stroke alert.

physical_exam.neuro: NIHSS 15 - right hemiparesis (arm 3/5, leg 4/5), right facial droop, expressive aphasia, right visual field cut, gaze deviation to left

imaging.ct_head: No hemorrhage, early loss of grey-white differentiation in left MCA territory
imaging.cta_head_neck: Left MCA M1 segment occlusion, no carotid stenosis

cases.explanation: Acute ischemic stroke in left MCA distribution: sudden onset focal neurological deficit (right hemiparesis, aphasia, gaze deviation). NIHSS 15 = moderate-severe. Risk factors: AFib (cardioembolic source), HTN. Within therapeutic window for both tPA (IV thrombolysis) and mechanical thrombectomy. Large vessel occlusion on CTA makes this thrombectomy candidate.
management_pearls: TIME IS BRAIN - Door-to-needle goal <60 minutes
tPA eligibility: <4.5 hours from symptom onset, no hemorrhage on CT, no contraindications
Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90mg): 10% bolus, 90% over 1 hour
BP management: Keep <185/110 before tPA, <180/105 after tPA
Mechanical thrombectomy: Large vessel occlusion + <6 hours (up to 24h with favorable imaging)
Stat neurology and neurointerventional consult
NPO, aspirin held x 24h post-tPA
Start anticoagulation for AFib after 24h (prevent recurrence)
Stroke unit admission for neuro checks q1-2h
Rehab evaluation early
cases.author: Dr. Stroke Neurology

cases.title: Man with Severe Epigastric Pain After Drinking
cases.presentation: 42-year-old man with severe upper abdominal pain radiating to back after binge drinking

history.chief_complaint: Worst stomach pain of my life
history.hpi: Severe epigastric pain started 6 hours ago after drinking heavily at party. Pain constant, boring, radiates to back. Multiple episodes of vomiting. Pain worse lying flat, better leaning forward. No relief with antacids.
history.pmh: Alcohol use disorder, prior episode of pancreatitis 2 years ago

physical_exam.abdomen: Epigastric tenderness without rebound, hypoactive bowel sounds, no Murphy's sign
physical_exam.other: No jaundice, no Grey-Turner or Cullen signs

imaging.ct_abdomen: Pancreatic edema and peripancreatic fat stranding, no necrosis or pseudocyst

cases.explanation: Acute pancreatitis diagnosis requires 2 of 3: (1) Characteristic pain ✓, (2) Lipase >3x ULN ✓, (3) Imaging findings ✓. Etiology is alcohol (GET SMASHED mnemonic). Pain radiating to back, worse supine, better leaning forward is classic. Hypocalcemia suggests more severe disease. No signs of necrotizing pancreatitis (no Grey-Turner/Cullen signs).
management_pearls: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation: Lactated Ringer's 250-500 mL/hr (decreases mortality)
Goal: UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr, Hct stable, BUN decreasing
Pain control: IV opioids (morphine, hydromorphone)
NPO initially, advance diet when pain improves (no need to wait for lipase normalization)
Ranson criteria at admission and 48h (predicts mortality)
ERCP only if gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis/obstruction
No routine antibiotics (unless infected necrosis)
Monitor for complications: necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess, ARDS, AKI
Alcohol cessation counseling and addiction treatment referral
references: ACG Guidelines for Management of Acute Pancreatitis
cases.author: Dr. Gastroenterology

cases.title: Woman with Decreased Urine Output
cases.presentation: 68-year-old woman with 2 days of decreased urine output, nausea, and confusion

history.hpi: Started new BP medication (lisinopril) 1 week ago. Developed diarrhea 3 days ago (viral gastroenteritis). Urine output markedly decreased past 2 days. Nausea, vomiting. Daughter notes confusion.

labs.urinalysis: Specific gravity 1.030, no protein, no blood, no casts

cases.explanation: Acute kidney injury (Cr increased 2.4x from baseline) with prerenal etiology. Risk factors: volume depletion (diarrhea, poor PO intake), ACE inhibitor (decreases GFR), NSAIDs (decrease renal perfusion), CKD. Physical exam shows hypovolemia (orthostasis, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia). Labs support prerenal: BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FENa <1%, urine Na <20, concentrated urine (high specific gravity). No hydronephrosis rules out postrenal.
management_pearls: STOP nephrotoxins: ACE inhibitor, NSAIDs, any other offending drugs
IV fluid resuscitation: Normal saline 500-1000 mL bolus, then maintenance
Monitor UOP, daily weights, strict I/Os
Trend Cr daily (should improve with fluids if prerenal)
Hyperkalemia management if K >6.0 or EKG changes: Calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, kayexalate
Avoid contrast, aminoglycosides, other nephrotoxins
Adjust medication doses for renal function
Urology consult only if hydronephrosis (postrenal)
Nephrology consult if: No improvement with fluids, intrinsic AKI, need dialysis (K >6.5, pH <7.1, volume overload, uremia)
references: Acute Kidney Injury: Diagnosis and Management
cases.author: Dr. Nephrology

cases.title: Woman with Sudden Difficulty Breathing After Bee Sting
cases.presentation: 32-year-old woman with sudden onset shortness of breath, throat tightness, and rash 5 minutes after bee sting

history.hpi: Stung by bee in garden 5 minutes ago. Immediately developed itching, then hives over whole body. Now complains throat feels tight, hard to swallow, difficulty breathing. Dizzy and nauseated. No prior bee sting reactions.

cases.explanation: Classic anaphylaxis: rapid onset (<minutes) of allergic symptoms involving ≥2 organ systems after allergen exposure (bee sting). Criteria met: (1) Skin involvement (urticaria, angioedema) + (2) Respiratory compromise (wheezing, stridor) + (3) Cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, tachycardia). Life-threatening emergency requiring immediate epinephrine.
management_pearls: EPINEPHRINE FIRST: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1:1000) in anterolateral thigh - DO NOT DELAY
Can repeat q5-15 min if no improvement
Call for help/activate emergency response
Position supine with legs elevated (or left lateral if pregnant/vomiting)
High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather
IV access: 1-2L NS bolus for hypotension
Adjunct therapy (NOT substitutes for epi): H1-blocker (diphenhydramine 50mg IV), H2-blocker (ranitidine 50mg IV), steroid (methylprednisolone 125mg IV), albuterol nebulizer
Monitor 4-6 hours minimum (biphasic reaction occurs in 20%)
Discharge with EpiPen x2 and education on use
Allergy/immunology referral for venom immunotherapy
cases.author: Dr. Emergency Medicine

cases.title: COPD Patient with Worsening Shortness of Breath
cases.presentation: 65-year-old man with known COPD presenting with 3 days of increased dyspnea, cough, and purulent sputum

history.hpi: COPD on home O2 (2L NC baseline). Developed URI symptoms 5 days ago. Progressive dyspnea, increased cough with yellow-green sputum, chest tightness. Using rescue inhaler every 2 hours without relief. No fever.

physical_exam.vitals: BP 145/85, HR 102, RR 28, O2 85% on 2L NC, Temp 98.6°F
physical_exam.general: Tripod position, using accessory muscles, speaking in short sentences
physical_exam.lungs: Diffuse expiratory wheezing, prolonged expiratory phase, decreased breath sounds

labs.abg: pH 7.32, pCO2 58, pO2 55, HCO3 30 (acute on chronic respiratory acidosis)

imaging.cxr: Hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, no consolidation or pneumothorax

cases.explanation: COPD exacerbation defined by acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal variation. Anthonisen criteria present: (1) Increased dyspnea ✓, (2) Increased sputum volume ✓, (3) Sputum purulence ✓ = Type 1 (most severe). ABG shows acute on chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. No evidence of pneumonia (afebrile, no consolidation on CXR). Triggered by viral URI.
management_pearls: Oxygen: Titrate to SpO2 88-92% (avoid CO2 retention from over-oxygenation)
Bronchodilators: Albuterol/ipratropium nebs q4h or continuous
Systemic steroids: Prednisone 40mg PO daily x 5 days (decreases recovery time, prevents relapse)
Antibiotics if purulent sputum: Azithromycin or doxycycline x 5 days
Consider BiPAP if: pH <7.35, pCO2 >45, RR >25, accessory muscle use
Intubation criteria: pH <7.25, declining mental status, BiPAP failure
Avoid sedatives (worsen hypoventilation)
Smoking cessation counseling
Pulmonary rehab referral
Ensure proper inhaler technique and adherence
cases.author: Dr. Pulmonary Medicine

cases.title: Man Vomiting Blood
cases.presentation: 52-year-old man with history of alcohol abuse presenting with hematemesis and melena

history.hpi: Two episodes of vomiting large amounts of bright red blood in past hour. Reports black, tarry stools x 2 days. Feeling dizzy and weak. Drinks heavily, history of chronic liver disease. No NSAIDs or anticoagulants.
history.pmh: Cirrhosis (alcohol-related), known esophageal varices, no prior bleeds

physical_exam.abdomen: Distended, fluid wave, mild tenderness, liver edge palpable, splenomegaly

cases.explanation: Variceal upper GI bleed in cirrhotic patient: hematemesis (bright red blood = active bleeding), melena, hemodynamic instability. Glasgow-Blatchford score high (predicts need for intervention). Risk factors: known varices, stopped beta-blocker prophylaxis. Signs of chronic liver disease: ascites, jaundice, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, spider angiomas. BUN:Cr ratio >30 suggests upper GI source. This is life-threatening emergency.
management_pearls: ABC resuscitation: 2 large-bore IVs (16-18G), aggressive crystalloid
Blood products: Transfuse PRBC goal Hgb 7-9 (over-transfusion increases portal pressure), FFP if INR >2.5, platelets if <50k
Octreotide 50 mcg bolus, then 50 mcg/hr infusion (decreases splanchnic blood flow)
Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 1g IV (reduces mortality, prevents SBP)
PPI: Pantoprazole 80mg bolus, then 8mg/hr infusion
URGENT EGD within 12 hours (preferably <6h if unstable)
Band ligation preferred over sclerotherapy for varices
If refractory: Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (temporizing), TIPS
Secondary prophylaxis: Non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol or carvedilol) + repeat EGD for surveillance
references: ACG Guidelines for Management of Variceal Hemorrhage
Upper GI Bleeding: Management and Outcomes
cases.author: Dr. Gastroenterology

cases.title: Elderly Woman with Shortness of Breath and Leg Swelling
cases.presentation: 78-year-old woman with progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and bilateral leg swelling over 1 week

history.chief_complaint: Can't breathe when I lie down
history.hpi: Progressive dyspnea over 1 week. Now can only sleep propped up on 3 pillows (orthopnea). Wakes up gasping for air at night (PND). Bilateral leg swelling. 10 lb weight gain. Cough with pink frothy sputum. Ran out of 'water pill' 2 weeks ago.
history.pmh: CHF with reduced EF 30%, CAD s/p MI, hypertension, diabetes
history.medications: Lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, furosemide (stopped 2 weeks ago)
history.social: Lives alone, diet non-compliant (ate salty foods)

imaging.cxr: Cardiomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions, Kerley B lines, cephalization

cases.explanation: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF): Framingham criteria met with multiple major criteria (PND, orthopnea, JVP elevated, S3 gallop, pulmonary edema on CXR) and minor criteria (edema, hepatomegaly). Precipitating factors: medication non-compliance (stopped furosemide), dietary indiscretion (high salt intake). BNP >500 confirms CHF. Wet and warm hemodynamic profile (volume overload without hypoperfusion).
management_pearls: Oxygen: Non-rebreather or BiPAP if severe respiratory distress
IV diuretics: Furosemide 40-80mg IV bolus (2.5x home dose if on chronic furosemide)
Goal: Net negative 1-2L daily, monitor strict I/Os, daily weights
ACE inhibitor: Continue home dose if normotensive (already on lisinopril)
Nitroglycerin: If HTN or flash pulmonary edema (reduces preload/afterload)
Avoid IV fluids (worsens volume overload)
Morphine controversial (may increase mortality)
Telemetry monitoring, troponin to rule out ACS
Once euvolemic: Restart GDMT (ACE-I, beta-blocker, aldosterone antagonist)
Discharge planning: Low-sodium diet (<2g/day), daily weights, medication adherence, cardiology follow-up
cases.author: Dr. Cardiology

cases.title: Young Man with Convulsions
cases.presentation: 24-year-old man brought by EMS actively seizing for 10 minutes, no improvement with 2 doses midazolam

history.hpi: Per EMS: Found seizing at home by roommate. Generalized tonic-clonic activity ongoing. Given midazolam 5mg IM x 2 without cessation. Total seizure time now 10 minutes. Known epileptic, ran out of medications 1 week ago.

imaging.ct_head: No acute findings (done after seizure controlled)

cases.explanation: Status epilepticus: continuous seizure >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without return to baseline. This is medical emergency with high mortality if not controlled rapidly. Cause: antiepileptic medication non-compliance (phenytoin level undetectable). Failed prehospital benzodiazepines = established status epilepticus requiring escalation. Complications: hypoxia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, cerebral edema.
management_pearls: TIME-BASED PROTOCOL:
0-5 min: ABC stabilization, check glucose (if low give D50), benzodiazepine
Lorazepam 4mg IV (or diazepam 10mg IV, or midazolam 10mg IM if no IV)
Can repeat once after 5 min if continues
5-20 min (established SE): Second-line AED
Fosphenytoin 20 PE/kg IV at max 150 PE/min OR
Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500mg) OR
Valproic acid 40 mg/kg IV
20-40 min (refractory SE): Continuous infusion + intubation
Propofol, midazolam, or pentobarbital drip
EEG monitoring for burst suppression
ICU admission for refractory cases
Identify and treat underlying cause
references: Neurocritical Care Society Status Epilepticus Guidelines
cases.author: Dr. Neurology

cases.title: Man with Painful Swollen Knee
cases.presentation: 56-year-old man with severe right knee pain, swelling, and fever, unable to bear weight

history.hpi: Woke up 2 days ago with right knee pain. Rapidly worsening, now can't walk on it. Knee hot, swollen, extremely painful with any movement. Fever and chills. No trauma. Had cortisone injection in same knee 1 week ago for osteoarthritis.

physical_exam.knee: Large effusion, erythema, warmth, exquisite tenderness, ROM severely limited by pain

labs.arthrocentesis: 60,000 WBC (90% PMNs), Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters, glucose 20 mg/dL (low), LDH elevated, no crystals

imaging.knee_xray: Joint effusion, no fracture, degenerative changes

cases.explanation: Septic arthritis: acute monoarticular arthritis with fever. Synovial fluid WBC >50,000 with PMN predominance strongly suggests bacterial infection. Gram stain positive for Staph aureus (most common organism). Risk factors: recent intra-articular injection, diabetes. This is orthopedic emergency - untreated leads to joint destruction. Cannot be gout (no crystals, WBC typically lower in gout).
management_pearls: URGENT ORTHOPEDIC CONSULT - This is surgical emergency
Arthrocentesis: Drain joint completely, send for cell count, Gram stain, culture
Empiric IV antibiotics immediately after cultures: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone (covers MRSA and GNRs)
Switch to organism-specific therapy when culture results available
Surgical drainage: Arthroscopic washout preferred (open if hip/shoulder)
Daily aspirations if not surgical candidate
IV antibiotics minimum 2 weeks, then PO to complete 4-6 weeks total
Monitor inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) - should downtrend
Physical therapy once infection controlled
Complications if untreated: cartilage destruction, osteomyelitis, sepsis
references: IDSA Guidelines for Septic Arthritis Management
Acute Septic Arthritis: Diagnosis and Treatment
cases.author: Dr. Orthopedic Surgery
